lessons.title: Why Traditional Risk Metrics Fall Short

children.text: You already know how to measure risk. Standard deviation, the Sharpe ratio, the Sortino ratio, maybe even the Calmar ratio if you have worked through a returns metrics course before this one. For a retail SIP investor, those tools are usually enough. For a quant researcher, a prop trading desk applicant, or a systematic trader running leveraged Nifty and Bank Nifty positions, they are not. This lesson is about why, and what a serious risk framework needs instead.
What a Single Number Cannot Tell You

Standard deviation answers one question: how far, on average, does a return wander from its mean? It says nothing about direction. A stock that gains 2% one day and loses 2% the next has exactly the same standard deviation as a stock that sits flat for ninety-nine sessions and then falls 20% on the hundredth. Any desk head who has run real capital through a crash will tell you those two stocks are not the same risk at all.

body.caption: Standard deviation of daily returns. It treats every deviation from the mean, up or down, exactly the same way.

body.text: A portfolio manager does not lose sleep over volatility. They lose sleep over the left tail, the days the book is down 8% and margin calls start landing. Volatility does not distinguish between the two sides of the distribution. A loss-focused risk measure has to.

children.text: The Assumption Hiding Inside Every Volatility Number

markDefs.definition: A return distribution where extreme outcomes occur more often than a normal distribution predicts.
A distribution where the tail on the downside is longer or fatter than the tail on the upside, meaning large losses are more likely than equally sized large gains.

children.text: Standard deviation, and everything built on it including the Sharpe ratio, works cleanly only if returns are roughly normally distributed, meaning extreme moves are rare in the specific way a bell curve predicts. Indian equity returns are not that well behaved. NSE data across Nifty, Bank Nifty, and most liquid single stocks shows
: large down moves happen more often than a normal distribution would predict, and the biggest single-day moves tend to fall on the downside.

children.text: Nifty 50 fell from a peak just above 12,400 in mid-January 2020 to an intraday low near 7,511 on 23 March 2020, a peak-to-trough decline of close to 40% in about ten weeks. On the morning of 23 March, the index fell so fast at the open that it tripped SEBI's market-wide circuit breaker, the mechanism that halts trading for 45 minutes when the index moves 10% from the previous close. Circuit breakers exist at 10%, 15%, and 20% precisely because moves of that size, while individually rare, are common enough across a market's history that regulators had to build a formal pause into the system. A normal distribution calibrated on an ordinary year would have called several of March 2020's daily moves close to impossible.

body.text: SEBI's market-wide circuit breakers trigger at index moves of 10%, 15%, and 20% from the previous close, with the length of the trading halt depending on the time of day the trigger hits. If your risk model has never produced a day this bad in its backtest, that is a sign the model has not seen enough history, not a sign the market cannot do it again.

children.text: Sharpe and Sortino Do Not Fix This Either

The Sharpe ratio divides excess return by standard deviation, so it inherits the same blind spot. The Sortino ratio is better, it only penalizes downside deviation, but both are ratios computed over a full return history. Neither one answers the specific question a risk desk, a broker's risk management team, or SEBI's own margining framework actually needs answered before the market opens tomorrow: how much rupee capital could this position lose, over a defined time horizon, at a stated confidence level, before you decide how much size to allow it.

body.title: What Volatility-Based Metrics Tell You vs What a Risk Desk Needs

columns.label: Sharpe, Sortino, Standard Deviation
points: Summarize an entire return history into a single number
Say nothing about a specific future day or a specific rupee amount
Assume the shape of past returns will hold going forward
Useful for comparing strategies after the fact

columns.label: What a Trading or Risk Desk Actually Needs
points: A rupee or percentage loss figure for a defined horizon, such as 1 day or 10 days
A stated confidence level, such as 95% or 99%, so everyone agrees what 'at risk' means
A number that can be set as a hard position or margin limit before the market opens
A framework that can be checked against how often it is actually breached

body.code:
import numpy as np

# daily returns for a Nifty-tracking position, illustrative placeholder
returns = np.array([...])  # load your own NSE daily close-to-close returns

mean = returns.mean()
std = returns.std()

# how many days moved more than 3 standard deviations from the mean?
extreme_days = np.sum(np.abs(returns - mean) > 3 * std)

print(f"Mean daily return: {mean:.4%}")
print(f"Std dev (volatility): {std:.4%}")
print(f"3-sigma+ days observed: {extreme_days} out of {len(returns)}")
body.caption: Pull your own daily close-to-close series, NSE bhavcopy data or Zerodha's Kite Connect historical API both work, and run this on Nifty, Bank Nifty, or any stock you trade. You will almost always find more extreme days than a normal distribution predicts.

body.title: The Position Sizing Problem
body.scenario: You are interning on a prop desk that trades Bank Nifty futures. Your strategy's daily returns have a standard deviation of 1.4%. The desk head asks you to size the position so that, on 99 out of 100 trading days, the loss stays under Rs 8 lakh. You have a Sharpe ratio for the strategy. You do not have anything else.
body.prompt: Can you answer the desk head's question using the Sharpe ratio or standard deviation alone? What is missing?
body.modelAnswer: No. Standard deviation tells you the typical size of a daily move, and Sharpe tells you return per unit of that typical move, but neither gives you a loss figure tied to a specific confidence level like '99 out of 100 days.' You need a measure explicitly built around a confidence level and a loss amount. That is exactly what Value at Risk is designed to answer, and it is where this course goes next.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Two stocks have the same standard deviation, but one has more negatively skewed returns with fatter tails. What does standard deviation alone fail to capture about that stock?
options: Its average return over the period
That its large losses are more frequent or more severe than a symmetric distribution would suggest
Its trading volume on the NSE
body.explanation: Standard deviation is a symmetric measure, it treats a 3% gain and a 3% loss identically. Skew and kurtosis, or better, the full loss distribution, are what reveal that the downside is worse than the upside.

body.text: Volatility measures how much a portfolio moves. It does not measure how much you can lose. The rest of this course is about closing that gap.

points: Standard deviation and Sharpe or Sortino are symmetric, history-summarizing measures. They were never built to answer 'how much could I lose, with what confidence, by when.'
Indian equity indices, including Nifty and Bank Nifty, show fat tails and negative skew: large down moves happen more often, and are more severe, than a normal distribution predicts.
March 2020 is the clearest recent evidence. SEBI's market-wide circuit breakers exist precisely because moves that a normal model would call near impossible do happen.

What a real risk desk needs is a measure with a stated rupee or percentage loss, a defined time horizon, and a stated confidence level. That is exactly what Value at Risk provides, starting in the next lesson.
